question: A pressure altimeter is essentially:

options.text: A barometer calibrated in feet according to the actual temperature of the day
A radio device that measures the time for a signal to return from the ground
An aneroid barometer whose scale is calibrated in feet according to the ISA

explanation: The altimeter measures static pressure with an aneroid capsule and converts it to height using the ISA pressure–height relationship. All altimeters therefore read the same for the same pressure and setting.

question: An aircraft is parked at a sea-level aerodrome with the altimeter reading zero. The pressure then falls by 10 hPa while the subscale is not touched. The altimeter will now read about:
explanation: The instrument cannot tell a fall in pressure from a climb. A 10 hPa fall at 27 ft per hPa makes it show about 270 ft, although the aircraft has not moved.

question: Unless otherwise stated, meteorology altimetry calculations use a height change of:
explanation: 27 ft per hPa is the ISA value near MSL and is the figure used in the meteorology syllabus calculations.

subtopic: Flying through pressure and temperature changes
question: An aircraft flies at a constant indicated altitude, without changing the subscale, from an area of high pressure into an area of low pressure. Its true altitude will:
explanation: The aircraft follows a constant-pressure surface, which dips towards low pressure. "High to low, look out below."

subtopic: Flying through pressure and temperature changes
question: An aircraft flies at a constant indicated altitude, without changing the subscale, from an area of low pressure into an area of high pressure. The altimeter will:
explanation: The constant-pressure surface rises towards higher pressure, so the aircraft climbs while the indication stays constant. True altitude is above indicated altitude.

subtopic: Flying through pressure and temperature changes
question: An aircraft flies at a constant indicated altitude from a warm area into a cold area. Its true altitude will:
explanation: Cold air is dense, so pressure levels are lower in cold air. Following a pressure level into cold air brings the aircraft lower. "Hot to cold, look out below."

subtopic: Flying through pressure and temperature changes
question: When the air below an aircraft is colder than ISA, its true altitude compared with the indicated altitude on QNH is:

options.text: Higher above 10 000 ft and lower below

explanation: The altimeter assumes ISA. In colder-than-standard air the pressure levels are compressed downward, so the aircraft is lower than indicated.

subtopic: Flying through pressure and temperature changes
question: When the air below an aircraft is warmer than ISA, its true altitude compared with the indicated altitude on QNH is:

options.text: Lower above the tropopause and higher below

explanation: Warm air expands the column, so pressure levels lie higher than in the ISA and the aircraft is above its indicated altitude.

subtopic: Flying through pressure and temperature changes
question: With the correct QNH set, an aircraft on the ground at an aerodrome where the temperature is ISA −20 will indicate:

options.text: Zero, because the cold air makes QNH equivalent to QFE
About 80 ft above the aerodrome elevation, because of the cold air
The aerodrome elevation, as the temperature error is zero at the datum
About 80 ft below the aerodrome elevation, because of the cold air

explanation: Temperature error grows with height above the setting datum. On the ground with QNH set there is no column to be in error, so the altimeter reads the elevation whatever the temperature.

subtopic: Flying through pressure and temperature changes
question: In the Northern Hemisphere an aircraft maintains a constant indicated altitude with a constant subscale setting and experiences starboard drift. Its true altitude is:

options.text: Changing only if the temperature changes

explanation: Starboard (right) drift in the Northern Hemisphere means the wind is from the left, so low pressure lies ahead. The pressure surfaces slope down and the aircraft descends with them.

subtopic: Flying through pressure and temperature changes
question: In the Southern Hemisphere an aircraft maintains a constant indicated altitude with a constant subscale setting and experiences starboard drift. Its true altitude is:

options.text: Changing only if the temperature changes

explanation: In the Southern Hemisphere low pressure is to the right of an observer with their back to the wind, so a wind from the left puts high pressure ahead. The aircraft climbs with the pressure surfaces.

question: With QFE set, the altimeter indicates:

options.text: Pressure altitude, and the aerodrome's pressure altitude on the ground
Height above the highest obstacle within 5 nm of the aerodrome
Altitude above mean sea level, and elevation on the ground
Height above the aerodrome, and zero on the ground there

explanation: QFE is aerodrome-level pressure, so the datum is the aerodrome itself.

question: With QNH set, the altimeter indicates:

options.text: Pressure altitude above the 1013 hPa datum
Altitude above MSL, and aerodrome elevation on the ground
True altitude, already corrected for temperature
Height above the aerodrome, and zero on the ground there

explanation: QNH reduces aerodrome pressure to MSL through the ISA, so the reading is altitude AMSL, subject to temperature error in flight.

question: With 1013 hPa set, the altimeter indicates:
explanation: The standard pressure setting references the ISA datum. Flight levels are pressure altitudes in hundreds of feet.

question: The regional (forecast) QNH for an altimeter setting region is:

options.text: The average QNH of all aerodromes in the region
The QNH at the main aerodrome of the region at the time of issue
The lowest QNH forecast for anywhere in the region over the next hour
The highest QNH forecast for the region

explanation: Using the lowest expected value means the actual pressure will be equal or higher, so the altimeter can only under-read: the aircraft is at or above its indicated altitude.

question: Why is the regional QNH chosen as the lowest forecast value rather than the average?

options.text: So that any error leaves the aircraft at or above its indicated altitude
Because the lowest QNH is always equal to the QFF in the region
Because aircraft fly faster in low pressure, needing more clearance
Because the lowest value is the easiest one to forecast accurately

explanation: If the setting is lower than the actual QNH, the altimeter under-reads. Errors therefore always place the aircraft higher than indicated, which preserves terrain clearance.

question: Altitude is defined as:

options.text: The vertical distance of a fixed object on the ground above MSL
The vertical distance of a level measured from a datum such as an aerodrome
The vertical distance of a level, point or object measured from MSL
A surface of constant pressure related to the 1013.25 hPa datum

explanation: Altitude is measured from MSL. Height is measured from a specified datum, and elevation is the altitude of a point on the Earth's surface.

question: Elevation is:

options.text: The vertical distance above MSL of a point on, or fixed to, the Earth's surface
The pressure altitude of an aircraft in flight, in hundreds of feet
The height of an aircraft above the highest obstacle on its route
The vertical distance of an aircraft in flight above the departure aerodrome

explanation: Aerodromes, obstacles and terrain have elevations. Aircraft in flight have altitudes or heights.

question: A flight level is:

options.text: A height above the departure aerodrome, measured on QFE
A true altitude that has been corrected for the temperature
An altitude above mean sea level, rounded to the nearest 500 ft for separation
A constant-pressure surface related to 1013.25 hPa, in hundreds of feet

explanation: Flight levels are pressure altitudes. FL350 corresponds to 35 000 ft on the standard setting.

question: The transition altitude is:

options.text: The airspace lying between the transition level and the transition altitude
The altitude at or below which vertical position is given as altitude on QNH
The lowest flight level available for use above the transition layer
The altitude above which the tropopause is normally found

explanation: Below and at the transition altitude, aircraft fly altitudes on QNH. Above it, in climb, the altimeter is set to 1013 hPa.

question: The transition level is:

options.text: The level at which QFE is set
The highest altitude available for use below the transition altitude
The lowest flight level available for use above the transition altitude

explanation: The transition level depends on the QNH. When the QNH is low, the flight levels sink and the transition level has to be higher.

question: The transition layer is:

options.text: The airspace below the transition altitude, where QNH is used
The airspace between the transition altitude and the transition level
The layer between FL100 and FL245 in controlled airspace
The airspace above the transition level, where 1013 hPa is used

explanation: Aircraft do not normally cruise in the transition layer. Climbing aircraft change to 1013 hPa at the transition altitude, and descending aircraft change to QNH at the transition level.

question: The transition altitude is 3000 ft and the QNH is 983 hPa. Using 27 ft per hPa, FL030 lies at about:

options.text: 3810 ft AMSL, above the transition altitude, so it is usable
3000 ft AMSL, exactly at the transition altitude
2190 ft AMSL, below the transition altitude, so it is not usable
3270 ft AMSL, just above the transition altitude

explanation: With QNH 30 hPa below 1013, the 1013 hPa datum lies 30 × 27 = 810 ft below MSL, so every flight level sits 810 ft lower than its nominal figure. FL030 is at about 2190 ft AMSL, below the transition altitude, so the transition level must be FL040 or higher.

question: An aircraft is on an aerodrome of elevation 500 ft. The altimeter is set to 1008 hPa but the actual QNH is 1015 hPa. Using 27 ft per hPa, the altimeter reads:
explanation: The setting is 7 hPa too low, so the altimeter under-reads by 7 × 27 = 189 ft: 500 − 189 = 311 ft.

question: An aircraft on an aerodrome of elevation 300 ft has 1020 hPa set. The actual QNH is 1005 hPa. Using 27 ft per hPa, the altimeter reads:
explanation: The setting is 15 hPa too high, so the altimeter over-reads by 15 × 27 = 405 ft: 300 + 405 = 705 ft. In flight this error would put the aircraft 405 ft lower than indicated.

question: An aircraft on an aerodrome of elevation 260 ft has 1009 hPa set and the altimeter reads 125 ft. Using 27 ft per hPa, the actual QNH is:
explanation: The altimeter under-reads by 260 − 125 = 135 ft = 5 hPa, so the setting is 5 hPa too low: QNH = 1009 + 5 = 1014 hPa.

question: An aircraft flies at an indicated 6000 ft with 1013 hPa set. The regional QNH is 995 hPa and the air is at ISA temperature. Using 27 ft per hPa, the true altitude is about:
explanation: The setting is 18 hPa higher than QNH, so the altimeter over-reads by 18 × 27 = 486 ft: 6000 − 486 = 5514 ft.

question: An aircraft flies at FL100 where the QNH is 1030 hPa and the temperature is ISA. Using 27 ft per hPa, its true altitude is about:
explanation: The 1013 hPa datum lies 17 × 27 = 459 ft above MSL when QNH is 1030 hPa, so the aircraft is 459 ft above its indicated pressure altitude.

question: An aircraft cruises at an indicated 4500 ft with 1022 hPa set, but the regional QNH is 1012 hPa. High ground of 4000 ft lies ahead. Assuming ISA temperatures and 27 ft per hPa, the aircraft will clear the ground by about:

options.text: It will not clear the ground

explanation: The setting is 10 hPa too high, so the altimeter over-reads by 270 ft. True altitude = 4500 − 270 = 4230 ft, giving 230 ft clearance.

question: An aircraft is on an aerodrome of elevation 1200 ft with the QFE of 970 hPa set. The altimeter reads:
explanation: With QFE set, the altimeter reads height above the aerodrome, which is zero on the ground.

question: An aerodrome has an elevation of 810 ft and its QNH is 1010 hPa. Using 27 ft per hPa, its QFE is:
explanation: 810 ÷ 27 = 30 hPa. The aerodrome is above MSL, so QFE = 1010 − 30 = 980 hPa.

question: An aerodrome has an elevation of 2000 ft and the QNH is 1003 hPa. Using 27 ft per hPa, its pressure altitude is:
explanation: QNH is 10 hPa below 1013, so the 1013 hPa datum lies 270 ft below MSL. Pressure altitude = 2000 + 270 = 2270 ft.

question: An aerodrome has an elevation of 1500 ft and the QNH is 1031 hPa. Using 27 ft per hPa, its pressure altitude is about:
explanation: QNH is 18 hPa above 1013, so pressure altitude = 1500 − 18 × 27 = 1500 − 486 = 1014 ft.

question: Density altitude increases with:
explanation: Both higher temperature and lower pressure reduce density, which corresponds to a higher ISA altitude.

question: An aerodrome is at pressure altitude 3000 ft and the temperature is +29°C. Using about 120 ft per °C of ISA deviation, the density altitude is approximately:
explanation: ISA at 3000 ft = 15 − 6 = +9°C, so the deviation is +20°C. Density altitude ≈ 3000 + 20 × 120 = 5400 ft.

question: The temperature error of an altimeter is proportional to:

options.text: The ISA deviation only, whatever the height of the aircraft
The difference between the QNH and the QFE at the aerodrome
The aircraft's true airspeed and the outside air temperature
The ISA deviation and the height above the setting datum

explanation: Each 1000 ft of air column between the datum and the aircraft contributes error in proportion to how far its temperature is from ISA.

question: A rule of thumb for altimeter temperature error is:

options.text: 4 ft per °C of ISA deviation per 1000 ft above the datum
27 ft per °C of ISA deviation, whatever the height
120 ft per °C of ISA deviation per 1000 ft above the datum
4 ft per hPa of pressure difference per 1000 ft

explanation: The error is about 0.4% of height per °C, which is 4 ft per °C per 1000 ft.

question: An aircraft indicates 3000 ft on QFE and the air below it is ISA −20. Its true height above the aerodrome is about:
explanation: Error = 4 × (−20) × 3 = −240 ft. Cold air puts the aircraft lower: 3000 − 240 = 2760 ft.

question: An aircraft indicates 8000 ft on QNH and the air below it is ISA +15. Its true altitude is about:
explanation: Error = 4 × 15 × 8 = +480 ft. Warm air puts the aircraft higher: 8000 + 480 = 8480 ft.

question: A decision height of 250 ft is used at an aerodrome where the temperature is ISA −30. At an indicated 250 ft, the true height is about:
explanation: Error = 4 × (−30) × 0.25 = −30 ft. The aircraft is 30 ft lower than indicated. In cold conditions the published DH or MDH must be increased.

question: When an approach is flown in temperatures well below ISA, the published decision or minimum descent altitude should be:

options.text: Used unchanged because QNH corrects for temperature
Increased to allow for the altimeter over-reading
Decreased because cold air improves performance

explanation: In cold air the aircraft is lower than indicated, so a cold-temperature correction is added to the minima to keep the intended obstacle clearance.

question: For a given ISA deviation, the altimeter temperature error during a final approach is:

options.text: Largest at the threshold, where the aircraft is closest to the ground
Largest at the start of the approach and decreasing towards the threshold
Constant throughout the approach, since the ISA deviation is constant
Zero above 1000 ft and increasing below that height to the threshold

explanation: The error is proportional to height above the datum, so it shrinks as the aircraft descends and is zero at the aerodrome with QNH (or QFE) set.

question: A route has a safety altitude of 6500 ft. The lowest forecast QNH is 993 hPa and the temperature is ISA −20. Using 27 ft per hPa and 4 ft per °C per 1000 ft, the lowest whole flight level that keeps the aircraft at or above the safety altitude is:
explanation: Pressure: 1013 − 993 = 20 hPa × 27 = 540 ft, giving 7040 ft indicated pressure altitude. Temperature: 4 × 20 × 7 ≈ 560 ft more, giving about 7600 ft. The next whole flight level above that is FL080.

question: An aircraft at FL200 crosses a mountain range. The QNH is 998 hPa and the mean temperature of the air below is ISA −15. Using 27 ft per hPa and 4 ft per °C per 1000 ft, its true altitude is about:
explanation: Pressure: 15 hPa × 27 = 405 ft lower, giving 19 595 ft. Temperature: 4 × (−15) × 20 = −1200 ft. True altitude ≈ 19 595 − 1200 = 18 395 ft. Both errors put the aircraft lower than indicated.

question: A pilot flies from an area of warm, high pressure into an area of cold, low pressure at a constant flight level. The combined effect on true altitude is:

options.text: Both errors lower the aircraft, so true altitude may fall a long way
Both errors raise the aircraft, so terrain clearance improves
The two errors cancel each other out, so true altitude is unchanged
Only the temperature effect matters, since flight levels ignore pressure

explanation: High to low and warm to cold both make the altimeter over-read. Together they can lead to a large loss of terrain clearance, especially in winter.

question: Which combination gives the greatest risk of an altimeter over-reading, so that the aircraft is lower than indicated?

options.text: High pressure and temperatures below ISA
Low pressure and temperatures below ISA
Low pressure and temperatures above ISA
High pressure and temperatures above ISA

explanation: Unless the subscale is updated, low pressure lowers the pressure surfaces, and cold air compresses the column. Both effects bring the true altitude below the indication.

question: At FL050, outside air temperature is +5°C. The altimeter is correctly set. The aircraft's true altitude is:

options.text: Impossible to determine without the dew point
About 200 ft above the pressure altitude, because of temperature error
Affected only by the QNH, as there is no temperature error at ISA
About 200 ft below the pressure altitude, because of temperature error

explanation: ISA at FL050 is 15 − 10 = +5°C, so there is no ISA deviation and no temperature error; only the difference between QNH and 1013 hPa affects true altitude.

question: Two aircraft cruise at FL330 on the same track, one in warm air and one in cold air. Their separation from each other is:

options.text: Lost, unless both aircraft set the regional QNH instead of 1013 hPa
Maintained, but only if the QNH along the route is exactly 1013 hPa
Lost, because the aircraft in cold air is about 1000 ft lower than the other
Maintained, as both fly the same pressure surface though their altitudes differ

explanation: All aircraft at flight levels use the same datum and fly constant-pressure surfaces, so vertical separation between them is preserved. Only terrain clearance is affected by true altitude.

question: An aircraft is on the ground at an aerodrome of elevation 1100 ft with the altimeter reading 1370 ft. The subscale shows 1013 hPa. Using 27 ft per hPa, the QNH is:
explanation: With 1013 set the altimeter shows pressure altitude, 270 ft above the elevation. 270 ÷ 27 = 10 hPa, so QNH is 10 hPa below standard: 1003 hPa.

question: An aircraft is at FL060 and the QNH is 1023 hPa. Using 27 ft per hPa and ISA temperatures, its altitude is about:
explanation: QNH is 10 hPa above 1013, so the 1013 hPa datum is 270 ft above MSL and the aircraft is 270 ft above its indicated pressure altitude.

question: Departing from an aerodrome with QNH 1030 hPa, a pilot forgets to change from QNH to 1013 hPa when climbing through the transition altitude and levels at an indicated FL100. The aircraft is actually at:
explanation: With 1030 set, the altimeter reads 17 × 27 ≈ 460 ft more than it would with 1013 set. The aircraft is therefore at about FL095, below its cleared level.

question: On descent, a pilot leaves 1013 hPa set below the transition level instead of setting the QNH of 990 hPa. At an indicated 3000 ft, the aircraft is actually at about:
explanation: With 1013 set, the altimeter over-reads by (1013 − 990) × 27 = 621 ft, so the aircraft is about 620 ft lower than indicated.

question: An aircraft maintains 5000 ft on a QNH of 1015 hPa and flies towards an area where the QNH is 995 hPa without updating the subscale. Over the second area its true altitude is about:
explanation: The pressure falls by 20 hPa, so the aircraft descends with the pressure surface by about 20 × 27 = 540 ft while still indicating 5000 ft.

question: An aircraft flies at an indicated 2000 ft on QFE over an aerodrome where the temperature is ISA +20. Its true height above the aerodrome is about:
explanation: Error = 4 × 20 × 2 = +160 ft. In warm air the aircraft is higher than indicated.

question: The temperature error of an altimeter depends on the air temperature:

options.text: Through the whole column between the datum and the aircraft
At the tropopause only, where the ISA becomes isothermal
At the surface only, measured at the departure aerodrome
At the aircraft's own level only, measured by the OAT probe

explanation: The altimeter's height scale assumes the ISA lapse rate for the whole column below. The mean temperature of that column determines the error.

question: Altimeter settings in reports are rounded down to the nearest whole hectopascal. The effect on an aircraft's indicated altitude is:

options.text: A slight under-reading, keeping the aircraft at or above its indicated altitude
A slight over-reading, putting the aircraft below its indicated altitude
An error of about 270 ft per hectopascal

explanation: A setting slightly lower than the true value makes the altimeter read slightly low, which is the safe direction.

question: Density altitude at an aerodrome is 4000 ft above its elevation. Compared with a standard day, take-off performance will be:

options.text: Better, as if the aerodrome were 4000 ft lower
Worse, as if the aerodrome were 4000 ft higher
Better because the air is warmer

explanation: Performance depends on density. A high density altitude means thin air, reducing lift and engine output.

question: In the Southern Hemisphere, an aircraft at constant indicated altitude has a strong wind from the right (port drift). Its true altitude is:

options.text: Increasing, because it is flying towards high pressure
Decreasing, because it is flying towards low pressure

explanation: In the Southern Hemisphere low pressure is on the right with your back to the wind. A wind from the right puts the low ahead of the aircraft, so the pressure surfaces slope down along its track.

question: The minimum safe flight level for a route sector must account for:

options.text: Only the elevation of the highest obstacle on the sector
The lowest forecast QNH and lowest forecast temperature on that sector
The highest forecast QNH and the highest forecast temperature on that sector
Only the QNH of the departure aerodrome at the time of take-off

explanation: Low pressure and low temperature both make the altimeter over-read, so the worst case for terrain clearance combines them.

question: A route sector has a safety altitude of 9000 ft. The lowest forecast QNH is 1003 hPa and the temperature is ISA. Using 27 ft per hPa, the lowest flight level giving at least the safety altitude is:
explanation: The 1013 hPa datum is 10 × 27 = 270 ft below MSL, so FL090 is only 8730 ft AMSL. 9270 ft of pressure altitude is needed; the next usable level above that is FL095.

question: Which altimeter setting would give an indicated reading of zero on landing at an aerodrome?
explanation: QFE is referenced to the aerodrome level. QNH gives elevation on landing, and 1013 hPa gives pressure altitude.

question: With QNH set, an aircraft indicates 2500 ft over a point of elevation 1200 ft. Assuming ISA, its height above that point is:
explanation: Height above the ground equals altitude minus ground elevation: 2500 − 1200 = 1300 ft.

question: When temperatures are very low, the correction for cold temperature should be applied to:

options.text: Only the published aerodrome elevation on the approach chart
Published minimum altitudes, such as DA/H, MDA/H and procedure altitudes
Only flight levels above FL250, where the air is coldest
Nothing, because the QNH setting already allows for low temperature

explanation: Cold air brings aircraft below their indicated altitudes, so published altitudes are raised to keep the required obstacle clearance.
